claim: N1-methylation of G37 is required for a subset of tRNAs to maintain the translational reading-frame.
source: N1-methylation of G37 is required for a subset of tRNAs to maintain the translational reading-frame.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Björk et al., 1989; Hagervall et al., 1993; Qian et al., 1998) in the introduction.

claim: Loss of m1G37 increases ribosomal +1 frameshifting.
source: While loss of m1G37 increases ribosomal +1 frameshifting, whether it incurs additional translational defects is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Gamper et al., 2015a; Gamper et al., 2021) in the introduction.

claim: m1G37 deficiency induces ribosome stalling at codons that are normally translated by m1G37-containing tRNAs.
source: Using E coli as a model, we show that m1G37 deficiency induces ribosome stalling at codons that are normally translated by m1G37-containing tRNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ribosome profiling data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Stalling occurs during decoding of affected codons at the ribosomal A site.
source: Stalling occurs during decoding of affected codons at the ribosomal A site, indicating a distinct mechanism than that of +1 frameshifting, which occurs after the affected codons leave the A site.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data showing pause scores when codons are in the A site (Figure 2).

claim: m1G37 deficiency reduces tRNA aminoacylation.
source: Enzyme- and cell-based assays show that m1G37 deficiency reduces tRNA aminoacylation and in some cases peptide-bond formation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinetic assays (Figure 3) and acid-urea gel analysis (Figure 4).

claim: m1G37 deficiency reduces peptide-bond formation in some cases.
source: Enzyme- and cell-based assays show that m1G37 deficiency reduces tRNA aminoacylation and in some cases peptide-bond formation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro peptide-bond formation assays showing reduced kobs for specific tRNA-codon pairs (Figure 3B).

claim: Changes of gene expression in m1G37 deficiency are similar to those in the stringent response.
source: We observe changes of gene expression in m1G37 deficiency similar to those in the stringent response that is typically induced by deficiency of amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing m1G37 deficiency with published stringent response data (Figure 6).

claim: m1G37 is essential for life.
source: N1-methylation of G37 in tRNA, generating m1G37 on the 3'-side of the anticodon, is a post-transcriptional modification that is essential for life (Björk et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: m1G37 is associated with all isoacceptors of tRNAPro across evolution.
source: It has been specifically associated across evolution with all isoacceptors of tRNAPro, which are species that share the same prolyl specificity of aminoacylation but differ in the primary sequence and in the anticodon triplet and yet collectively decode the Pro CCN codons (N = A, C, G, and U).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations (Björk et al., 2001).

claim: m1G37 is conserved in the CCG isoacceptor of tRNAArg.
source: Similarly, m1G37 is conserved in the CCG isoacceptor of tRNAArg(tRNAArg(CCG)), with the anticodon CCG for pairing with the CGG codon, and it is conserved in isoacceptors tRNALeu(GAG), tRNALeu(UAG), and tRNALeu(CAG) for pairing with CUU and CUC codons (CU[C/U]) and CU[A/G] codons, respectively (Björk et al., 2001; Li et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: m1G37 is conserved in isoacceptors tRNALeu(GAG), tRNALeu(UAG), and tRNALeu(CAG).
source: Similarly, m1G37 is conserved in the CCG isoacceptor of tRNAArg(tRNAArg(CCG)), with the anticodon CCG for pairing with the CGG codon, and it is conserved in isoacceptors tRNALeu(GAG), tRNALeu(UAG), and tRNALeu(CAG) for pairing with CUU and CUC codons (CU[C/U]) and CU[A/G] codons, respectively (Björk et al., 2001; Li et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Elimination of the enzyme responsible for m1G37 methylation causes cell death in yeast and bacteria.
source: The m1G37 methylation of tRNA is required for cell growth and viability; elimination of the enzyme responsible for the methylation causes cell death in yeast and in bacteria (Björk et al., 2007; Björk et al., 2001; Masuda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The established function of m1G37 is to maintain the translational reading-frame during protein synthesis.
source: The established function of m1G37 is to maintain the translational reading-frame during protein synthesis (Björk et al., 1989; Hagervall et al., 1993; Qian et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of m1G37 elevates frequencies of ribosomal +1 frameshifting in kinetic assays with reconstituted E. coli ribosomes.
source: Loss of m1G37 elevates frequencies of ribosomal +1 frameshifting in kinetic assays with reconstituted E. coli ribosomes (Gamper et al., 2015a), and in cell-based assays in E. coli and Salmonella (Gamper et al., 2021; Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of m1G37 elevates frequencies of ribosomal +1 frameshifting in cell-based assays in E. coli and Salmonella.
source: Loss of m1G37 elevates frequencies of ribosomal +1 frameshifting in kinetic assays with reconstituted E. coli ribosomes (Gamper et al., 2015a), and in cell-based assays in E. coli and Salmonella (Gamper et al., 2021; Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Non-methylated tRNAs occupy the correct reading-frame in X-ray crystal structures.
source: While non-methylated tRNAs were thought to pair incorrectly in the ribosomal A site (the aminoacyl-tRNA [aa-tRNA] binding site) during decoding (Roth, 1981), they were found to occupy the correct reading-frame in X-ray crystal structures and in kinetic assays (Gamper et al., 2021; Maehigashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Non-methylated tRNAs occupy the correct reading-frame in kinetic assays.
source: While non-methylated tRNAs were thought to pair incorrectly in the ribosomal A site (the aminoacyl-tRNA [aa-tRNA] binding site) during decoding (Roth, 1981), they were found to occupy the correct reading-frame in X-ray crystal structures and in kinetic assays (Gamper et al., 2021; Maehigashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: A frameshift-prone tRNA lacking m1G37 undergoes +1 frameshifting during translocation from the A site to the P site.
source: A frameshift-prone tRNA, containing the natural anticodon loop but lacking m1G37, is shown in kinetic assays to undergo +1 frameshifting during translocation from the A site to the P site, or during occupancy in the P site next to an empty A site (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: A frameshift-prone tRNA lacking m1G37 undergoes +1 frameshifting during occupancy in the P site next to an empty A site.
source: A frameshift-prone tRNA, containing the natural anticodon loop but lacking m1G37, is shown in kinetic assays to undergo +1 frameshifting during translocation from the A site to the P site, or during occupancy in the P site next to an empty A site (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: A genetically isolated high-efficiency +1-frameshifting tRNA undergoes +1 frameshifting during translocation.
source: A genetically isolated high-efficiency +1-frameshifting tRNA, containing an expanded anticodon loop, is also shown in kinetic assays to undergo +1 frameshifting during translocation (Gamper et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: m1G37 stabilizes tRNA on an mRNA codon that is prone to frameshifting.
source: In these latter structures, while m1G37 stabilizes the tRNA on an mRNA codon that is prone to frameshifting, loss of m1G37 destabilizes the tRNA-ribosome interaction and induces +1 frameshifting within large conformational changes of the ribosome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referring to X-ray crystal structures (Hoffer et al., 2020).

claim: Loss of m1G37 destabilizes the tRNA-ribosome interaction and induces +1 frameshifting within large conformational changes of the ribosome.
source: In these latter structures, while m1G37 stabilizes the tRNA on an mRNA codon that is prone to frameshifting, loss of m1G37 destabilizes the tRNA-ribosome interaction and induces +1 frameshifting within large conformational changes of the ribosome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referring to X-ray crystal structures (Hoffer et al., 2020).

claim: trmD-deg cells rapidly lost viability when clpXP expression was turned on.
source: Analysis of a serial dilution of each strain confirmed that trmD-deg cells rapidly lost viability, whereas trmD-cont cells retained viability (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the spot dilution assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: trmD-cont cells retained viability when clpXP expression was turned on.
source: Analysis of a serial dilution of each strain confirmed that trmD-deg cells rapidly lost viability, whereas trmD-cont cells retained viability (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the spot dilution assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The level of TrmD protein drastically decreased in 30 min after the first dilution into fresh LB + Ara in trmD-deg strain.
source: Although the growth defect of the trmD-deg strain only manifested in the third cycle of dilution, the level of TrmD protein drastically decreased in 30 min after the first dilution into fresh LB + Ara (as in Figure 1B), whereas that in the trmD-cont strain remained stable up to 90 min (Figure 1C) and longer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TrmD protein level in trmD-cont strain remained stable up to 90 min.
source: Although the growth defect of the trmD-deg strain only manifested in the third cycle of dilution, the level of TrmD protein drastically decreased in 30 min after the first dilution into fresh LB + Ara (as in Figure 1B), whereas that in the trmD-cont strain remained stable up to 90 min (Figure 1C) and longer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the time of cell harvest, the m1G37 level was 100% for trmD-cont cells at T = 3 hr.
source: At the time of cell harvest, the m1G37 level was 100% for trmD-cont cells at T = 3 hr, but was below 25% for trmD-deg cells at T = 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by primer-extension inhibition analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At the time of cell harvest, the m1G37 level was below 25% for trmD-deg cells at T = 4 hr.
source: At the time of cell harvest, the m1G37 level was 100% for trmD-cont cells at T = 3 hr, but was below 25% for trmD-deg cells at T = 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by primer-extension inhibition analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ribosome density at Pro codons was dramatically increased in m1G37 deficiency, showing an increase in the pause score from 1.4 in trmD-cont cells to 3.5 in trmD-deg cells.
source: Most notably, ribosome density at Pro codons was dramatically increased in m1G37 deficiency, showing an increase in the pause score from 1.4 in trmD-cont cells to 3.5 in trmD-deg cells (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pause score at Pro codons increased from 1.2 in trmD-WT (trm5–) cells to 2.5 in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells.
source: Similarly, the pause score at Pro codons increased from 1.2 in trmD-WT (trm5–) cells to 2.5 in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Elevated pause scores on the CGG codon were observed in m1G37 deficiency, increasing from 1.0 in control cells to 3.0 in trmD-deg cells and in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells.
source: Also, we observed elevated pause scores on the CGG codon (in green) in m1G37 deficiency, increasing from 1.0 in control cells to 3.0 in trmD-deg cells and in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A small increase of the pause score at the Leu codon CUA was observed in m1G37 deficiency at 1.4 relative to the pause score of 1.0 in control samples.
source: Additionally, we observed a small increase of the pause score at the Leu codon CUA in m1G37 deficiency at 1.4 relative to the pause score of 1.0 in control samples (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pauses are primarily in the A site, due to defects in decoding associated with m1G37 deficiency.
source: We conclude that pauses are primarily in the A site, due to defects in decoding associated with m1G37 deficiency.
evidence: This conclusion is based on ribosome profiling data showing the highest pause scores when codons are in the A site (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Increased ribosome density ~25 nt upstream of affected codons in trmD-deg relative to trmD-cont samples indicates collision of an upstream ribosome with a paused ribosome.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased ribosome density ~25 nt upstream of affected codons in trmD-deg relative to trmD-cont samples (Figure 2C–D, top). This distance is roughly equivalent to the footprint length of a single ribosome, indicating that the increased density was due to collision of an upstream ribosome with a paused ribosome that was struggling to decode an affected codon.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2C-D and inference about ribosome footprint size.

claim: For all three isoacceptors of tRNAPro, the catalytic efficiency kcat/Km was decreased from the m1G37-state to the G37-state by 3- to 10-fold.
source: For all three isoacceptors of tRNAPro, the catalytic efficiency kcat/Km was decreased from the m1G37-state to the G37-state by 3- to 10-fold (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro aminoacylation kinetic assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduction in kcat/Km for tRNAPro aminoacylation was driven by an increase in Km for all three tRNAs.
source: The reduction in kcat/Km was driven by an increase in Km for all three tRNAs, indicating that m1G37 may be important for binding of each tRNA to ProRS (Figure 3—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic parameters shown in Figure 3—source data 1A.

claim: The largest decrease in kcat/Km (10-fold) upon loss of m1G37 was observed for the UGG isoacceptor of tRNAPro.
source: The largest decrease in kcat/Km (10-fold) upon loss of m1G37 was observed for the UGG isoacceptor.
evidence: This is supported by aminoacylation kinetic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The UGG isoacceptor of tRNAPro is required for cell growth and survival.
source: Unique among the isoacceptors of tRNAPro, the UGG isoacceptor is required for cell growth and survival (Nasvall et al., 2004) and is most critically dependent on m1G37 for maintaining the translational reading-frame (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Aminoacylation reaction with the m1G37-state tRNAPro(UGG) has the same kcat/Km values as the native-state tRNA.
source: The critical role that m1G37 plays in the UGG isoacceptor was further highlighted by the finding that aminoacylation reaction with the m1G37-state tRNA has the same kcat/Km values as the native-state tRNA (Figure 3—source data 1A), indicating that all other post-transcriptional modifications played little or no role in aminoacylation.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3—source data 1A.

claim: The kcat/Km of aminoacylation of tRNAArg(CCG) was decreased from the m1G37-state to the G37-state by 5.6-fold.
source: Aminoacylation of the tRNAArg(CCG) isoacceptor with Arg was performed with purified E. coli ArgRS under steady-state multi-turnover conditions. The kcat/Km of aminoacylation was decreased from the m1G37-state to the G37-sate by 5.6-fold (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro aminoacylation kinetic assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decrease in kcat/Km for tRNAArg(CCG) aminoacylation was largely driven by a loss in kcat.
source: This decrease was largely driven by a loss in kcat (Figure 3—source data 1A), indicating that m1G37 contributed to catalysis, which is a different effect than that observed for tRNAPro, where loss of m1G37 likely reduced tRNA binding to ProRS.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic parameters shown in Figure 3—source data 1A.

claim: Loss of m1G37 only had a significant effect on kobs with the UGG isoacceptor of tRNAPro at the CCC codon, decreasing kobs by 14.4-fold from the m1G37-state to the G37-state.
source: The results of these assays showed that, of all of the tested anticodon-codon pairs, loss of m1G37 only had a significant effect on kobs with the UGG isoacceptor at the CCC codon, decreasing kobs by 14.4-fold from the m1G37-state to the G37-state (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by peptide-bond formation assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of m1G37 reduced the activity of dipeptide formation at the A site for tRNAArg(CCG) at the CGG codon by 14.3-fold from the m1G37-state to the G37-state.
source: Likewise, the CCG isoacceptor of tRNAArg was assayed at the cognate codon CGG, showing a significant decrease of kobs by 14.3-fold from the m1G37-state to the G37-state (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by peptide-bond formation assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tRNAPro(UGG) had reduced aa-tRNA levels in m1G37 deficiency, decreasing from 84% to 68%.
source: Northern blots with probes against tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CCG) showed that both had reduced aa-tRNA levels, decreasing from 84% to 68% and from 74% to 62% respectively in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 4A, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by acid-urea gel Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: tRNAArg(CCG) had reduced aa-tRNA levels in m1G37 deficiency, decreasing from 74% to 62%.
source: Northern blots with probes against tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CCG) showed that both had reduced aa-tRNA levels, decreasing from 84% to 68% and from 74% to 62% respectively in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 4A, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by acid-urea gel Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The aa-tRNA level of tRNATyr(QUA) was similar (78% vs. 81%) whether m1G37 was abundant or deficient.
source: Acid-urea gel analysis of E. coli tRNATyr(QUA) (Q: queuosine), which contains ms2i6A37 (2-methyl-thio-N6-isopentenyl adenosine) and is not methylated by TrmD, showed that its aa-tRNA level was similar (78% vs. 81%) whether m1G37 was abundant or deficient (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by acid-urea gel Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 4A and serves as a control.

claim: The expression level of proS and argS was unaffected by m1G37 deficiency.
source: RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data showed that the expression level of these two enzymes was unaffected by m1G37 deficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cell lysates in m1G37-abundant (trm5+) and m1G37-deficient (trm5–) conditions exhibited a similar aminoacylation activity when assayed with the methylated m1G37-tRNAPro(UGG) or m1G37-tRNAArg(CCG).
source: Moreover, cell lysates in m1G37-abundant (trm5+) and m1G37-deficient (trm5–) conditions exhibited a similar aminoacylation activity when assayed with the methylated m1G37-tRNAPro(UGG) or m1G37-tRNAArg(CCG) (Figure 4C, left and middle panels), indicating that the enzymatic activity of proS and argS was similar between the two growth conditions.
evidence: This is supported by aminoacylation assays on cell lysates shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The lost aminoacylation of tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CGG) in m1G37 deficiency was recovered by over-expression of proS and argS in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells.
source: Additional data showed that the lost aminoacylation of tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CGG) in m1G37 deficiency was recovered by over-expression of proS and argS in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells (Figure 4A, left and middle panels, the third lane of each).
evidence: This is supported by acid-urea gel Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: m1G37-deficient cells (trmD-KO (trm5–)) grew poorly with an empty plasmid, but improved viability upon over-expression of proS or argS.
source: Indeed, while control cells in m1G37-abundant conditions (trmD-KO (trm5+)) grew robustly, with or without over-expression of a plasmid-borne proS or argS, m1G37-deficient cells (trmD-KO (trm5–)) grew poorly with an empty plasmid, but improved viability upon over-expression of proS or argS (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution viability assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The recovery of cell viability upon over-expression of proS approached that of the positive control (trmD-KO (trm5+)), whereas that of over-expression of argS was much weaker.
source: Notably, while the loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency was similar to tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CCG) in cell lysates (Figure 4A, left and middle panels), the recovery of cell viability upon over-expression of proS approached that of the positive control (trmD-KO (trm5+)), whereas that of over-expression of argS was much weaker (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the viability data in Figure 4D.

claim: It is the loss of aminoacylation of tRNAPro species that is the driver for limiting cell growth under m1G37 deficiency.
source: This indicates that it is the loss of aminoacylation of tRNAPro species that is the driver for limiting cell growth under m1G37 deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue effects of proS vs argS over-expression on cell viability.

claim: 220 genes had more than 2-fold higher expression (p < 0.01) in the trmD-deg strain.
source: We found 220 genes with more than 2-fold higher expression (p < 0.01) in the trmD-deg strain (shown in red, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analyzed by DESeq shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 166 genes were repressed by more than 2-fold (p < 0.01) in the trmD-deg strain.
source: Conversely, we identified 166 genes that were repressed by more than 2-fold (p < 0.01, colored in blue, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analyzed by DESeq shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 71 genes had higher levels of apparent ribosome occupancy (1.7- to 6.5-fold increase) in the trmD-deg strain relative to the trmD-cont strain (p < 0.01).
source: Using the Xtail algorithm (Xiao et al., 2016) to identify changes in ribosome occupancy (RO = Ribo-seq density/RNA-seq density), we found 71 genes with higher levels of apparent ribosome occupancy (1.7- to 6.5-fold increase) in the trmD-deg strain relative to the trmD-cont strain (p < 0.01, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling and RNA-seq data analyzed by Xtail shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Many of the genes with higher RNA levels upon TrmD depletion are involved in amino acid biosynthesis and transport.
source: Many of the genes with higher RNA levels upon TrmD depletion are involved in amino acid biosynthesis and transport (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Induction of the Leu operon (leuA, leuB, leuC, and leuD) was particularly strong (~16-fold) in m1G37 deficiency.
source: For example, induction of the Leu operon (leuA, leuB, leuC, and leuD) was particularly strong (~16-fold).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Ribosomal pausing was observed in leuL at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in m1G37 deficiency.
source: We observed ribosomal pausing in leuL at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 5D), consistent with our observation of ribosome pausing at CUA codons (Figure 2B), suggesting that the pausing would prevent transcriptional termination and allow transcription elongation into the downstream Leu biosynthetic genes, resulting in elevated RNA levels.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the control trmD-cont strain, the average RNA-seq density decreased 29-fold from the leuL leader sequence to the first gene in the operon (leuA).
source: In agreement with this transcriptional attenuation mechanism, we observed in the control trmD-cont strain efficient transcriptional termination downstream of leuL, where the average RNA-seq density (adjusted for length) decreased 29-fold from the leuL leader sequence to the first gene in the operon (leuA), whereas we observed in the trmD-deg strain only a 4-fold decrease (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the trmD-deg strain, the average RNA-seq density decreased only 4-fold from the leuL leader sequence to leuA.
source: In agreement with this transcriptional attenuation mechanism, we observed in the control trmD-cont strain efficient transcriptional termination downstream of leuL, where the average RNA-seq density (adjusted for length) decreased 29-fold from the leuL leader sequence to the first gene in the operon (leuA), whereas we observed in the trmD-deg strain only a 4-fold decrease (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Strong ribosome pauses at two consecutive Pro codons CCA-CCG were observed in ilvL in m1G37 deficiency.
source: Although this genetic switch has evolved to sense changes in levels of aa-tRNAs associated with the amino acids produced by the downstream genes, we instead observed strong ribosome pauses at two consecutive Pro codons CCA-CCG in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the control strain, a 45-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density was observed from the region around ilvL to the first half of the downstream ilvG gene.
source: Indeed, while we observed in the control strain a 45-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density from the region around ilvL to the first half of the downstream ilvG gene, we observed in the trmD-deg strain only a 9-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the trmD-deg strain, only a 9-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density was observed from the region around ilvL to the first half of the downstream ilvG gene.
source: Indeed, while we observed in the control strain a 45-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density from the region around ilvL to the first half of the downstream ilvG gene, we observed in the trmD-deg strain only a 9-fold decrease in the RNA-seq density (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Upon expression of the WT reporter construct, m1G37 deficiency in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells elevated the nLuc readout by 11.5-fold relative to control cells.
source: Upon expression of the WT reporter construct, m1G37 deficiency in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells elevated the nLuc readout by 11.5-fold relative to control cells, consistent with the notion that ribosome stalling at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in leuL prevents transcriptional termination and allows transcription of the downstream leuA-nLuc fusion.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A smaller activation during m1G37 deficiency (only 2.7-fold) was observed with a second nLuc reporter where the four consecutive Leu CUA codons were changed to Leu UUA codons.
source: In contrast, a smaller activation during m1G37 deficiency (only 2.7-fold) was observed with a second nLuc reporter where the four consecutive Leu CUA codons were changed to Leu UUA codons, which do not require m1G37 for translation.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: With the wild-type ilvL sequence, ilvG was up-regulated 3.1-fold in m1G37-deficient trmD-KO (trm5–) cells relative to m1G37-abundant trmD-KO (trm5+) cells.
source: With the wild-type ilvL sequence, ilvG was up-regulated 3.1-fold in m1G37-deficient trmD-KO (trm5–) cells relative to m1G37-abundant trmD-KO (trm5+) cells (left panel, bar 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No increase in ilvG expression was observed for the mutant ilvL sequence where Pro codons were changed to Ala codons.
source: In contrast, no increase was observed for the mutant ilvL sequence (right panel, bar 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Over-expression of proS in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells with the wild-type ilvL leader sequence reduced the activation of ilvG from 3.1-fold to 1.5-fold.
source: We found that over-expression of proS in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells with the wild-type ilvL leader sequence reduced the activation of ilvG from 3.1-fold to 1.5-fold (left panel, bars 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The biosynthetic pathways for Trp, His, and Cys were highly up-regulated in the trmD-deg strain.
source: In addition to Leu, Ile, and Val, the biosynthetic pathways for Trp, His, and Cys were highly up-regulated in the trmD-deg strain (Figure 5C), even though there is no evidence of ribosome stalling at the 5'-leader of the relevant operons.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genes that were down-regulated upon relA over-expression were also down-regulated in m1G37 deficiency (log2(median) = –0.36; t-test p = 8.9 × 10–15).
source: Using these same sets of genes, we found in our RNA-seq data that genes that were down-regulated upon relA over-expression were also down-regulated in m1G37 deficiency (log2(median) = –0.36; t-test p = 8.9 × 10–15) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data with published stringent response data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Genes that were up-regulated in relA over-expression were also up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency (log2(median) = 0.29; t-test p = 2.3 × 10–11).
source: Likewise, genes that were up-regulated in relA over-expression were also up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 6A), although the extent of up-regulation in m1G37 deficiency was smaller (log2(median) = 0.29; t-test p = 2.3 × 10–11).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data with published stringent response data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 89 genes associated with amino acid biosynthesis were more highly expressed than other genes upon relA over-expression (log2(median) = 0.59, Mann-Whitney p = 4.8 × 10–12).
source: As expected, the published RNA-seq data upon relA over-expression showed that 89 genes associated with amino acid biosynthesis in the EcoCyc database were more highly expressed than other genes (log2(median) = 0.59, Mann-Whitney p = 4.8 × 10–12).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RNA-seq data from the stringent response.

claim: 89 genes associated with amino acid biosynthesis were up-regulated to a similar extent in m1G37 deficiency (log2(median) = 0.58, Mann-Whitney p = 1.2 × 10–8).
source: Intriguingly, we found that these genes were also up-regulated to a similar extent in m1G37 deficiency (log2(median) = 0.58, Mann-Whitney p = 1.2 × 10–8) (Figure 6B), consistent with the enrichment of these genes in our GO annotation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 47 ribosome protein genes were down-regulated upon relA over-expression (log2(median) = –1.48, Mann-Whitney p = 1.6 × 10–24).
source: Likewise, 47 ribosome protein genes were down-regulated upon relA over-expression (log2(median) = –1.48, Mann-Whitney p = 1.6 × 10–24) and they were also down-regulated in m1G37 deficiency, although to a lesser extent (log2(median) = –0.64, Mann-Whitney p = 1.1 × 10–12) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RNA-seq data from the stringent response.

claim: 47 ribosome protein genes were down-regulated in m1G37 deficiency, although to a lesser extent (log2(median) = –0.64, Mann-Whitney p = 1.1 × 10–12).
source: Likewise, 47 ribosome protein genes were down-regulated upon relA over-expression (log2(median) = –1.48, Mann-Whitney p = 1.6 × 10–24) and they were also down-regulated in m1G37 deficiency, although to a lesser extent (log2(median) = –0.64, Mann-Whitney p = 1.1 × 10–12) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 10 genes associated with the TCA cycle were significantly up-regulated in the trmD-deg strain, making this pathway the most enriched in the GO terms.
source: For example, 10 genes associated with the TCA cycle were significantly up-regulated in the trmD-deg strain, making this pathway the most enriched in the GO terms (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genes in the glyoxylate cycle are up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency.
source: Genes in the glyoxylate cycle are also up-regulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results section on metabolic changes.

claim: Enzymes for fatty acid oxidation are highly up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency.
source: The two-carbon units entering the TCA cycle likely arise primarily from fatty acid oxidation, whose enzymes are highly up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency, as opposed to the glycolysis pathway, whose genes are strongly repressed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genes in the glycolysis pathway are strongly repressed in m1G37 deficiency.
source: The two-carbon units entering the TCA cycle likely arise primarily from fatty acid oxidation, whose enzymes are highly up-regulated in m1G37 deficiency, as opposed to the glycolysis pathway, whose genes are strongly repressed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: m1G37 deficiency shifts metabolism away from consuming Glc toward consuming fatty acids.
source: Thus, it appears that m1G37 deficiency shifts metabolism away from consuming Glc toward consuming fatty acids and that cells prioritize building up metabolic intermediates to support amino acid biogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the patterns of gene expression changes in metabolic pathways.

claim: Cells in m1G37 deficiency prioritize building up metabolic intermediates to support amino acid biogenesis.
source: Thus, it appears that m1G37 deficiency shifts metabolism away from consuming Glc toward consuming fatty acids and that cells prioritize building up metabolic intermediates to support amino acid biogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the patterns of gene expression changes in metabolic pathways.

claim: TrmD is ranked as a high-priority antibacterial target.
source: This genome-wide view is important, because TrmD is ranked as a high-priority antibacterial target (White and Kell, 2004), due to its fundamental distinction from Trm5, and its conservation throughout the bacterial domain, essentiality for bacterial life, and possession of a small molecule-binding site for drug targeting.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The small molecule-binding site in TrmD consists of a protein topological knot-fold that holds the methyl donor S-adenosyl methionine in an unusual shape.
source: The small molecule-binding site in TrmD is unique, consisting of a protein topological knot-fold that holds the methyl donor S-adenosyl methionine in an unusual shape (Ahn et al., 2003; Elkins et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2015), which is different from that in Trm5 and in most other methyl transferases (Goto-Ito et al., 2009), indicating the possibility to explore novel chemical space and diversity of drugs targeting TrmD.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: TrmD deficiency can disrupt the double-membrane cell-envelope structure of Gram-negative bacteria, thus facilitating permeability of multiple drugs into cells, preventing efflux of these drugs, and accelerating bactericidal action.
source: Additionally, we have shown that TrmD deficiency can disrupt the double-membrane cell-envelope structure of Gram-negative bacteria, thus facilitating permeability of multiple drugs into cells, preventing efflux of these drugs, and accelerating bactericidal action (Masuda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ribosome stalling can be prolonged if a subset of the affected tRNAs is unable to perform peptide-bond formation in the A site, leading to ribosome collisions that increase the frequency of frameshifting.
source: Ribosome stalling can be prolonged if a subset of the affected tRNAs is unable to perform peptide-bond formation in the A site, leading to ribosome collisions that increase the frequency of frameshifting (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: m1G37-deficient tRNAs would induce +1 frameshifting during translocation to the P site and destabilize interaction with the ribosomal P site, leading to premature fall-off from the ribosome and termination of protein synthesis.
source: Even if some of the m1G37-deficient tRNAs manage to enter the A site and participate in peptide-bond formation, they would induce +1 frameshifting during translocation to the P site and destabilize interaction with the ribosomal P site (Hoffer et al., 2020), leading to premature fall-off from the ribosome and termination of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency is not due to the loss of ProRS or ArgRS in cells.
source: While the loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency is not due to the loss of ProRS or ArgRS in cells, it can be restored by over-expression of either enzyme, which improves cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency can be restored by over-expression of ProRS or ArgRS, which improves cell viability.
source: While the loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency is not due to the loss of ProRS or ArgRS in cells, it can be restored by over-expression of either enzyme, which improves cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4A and 4D.

claim: The loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency, and consequently the accumulation of uncharged tRNAs, is the underlying basis of ribosome stalling that induces significant changes in gene expression.
source: These results clearly demonstrate that the loss of aminoacylation in m1G37 deficiency, and consequently the accumulation of uncharged tRNAs, is the underlying basis of ribosome stalling that induces significant changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The binding of deacylated tRNA to the A site is known to induce (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on the ribosome.
source: These changes certainly make sense given that we see higher levels of deacylated tRNAs accumulating in m1G37 deficiency and that the binding of deacylated tRNA to the A site is known to induce (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA on the ribosome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on established knowledge of the stringent response.

claim: In yeast, loss of the 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl (mcm5) and/or the 2-thio (s2) groups from the normal mcm5s2U34-state tRNA activates the GCN4-mediated pathway.
source: In yeast, loss of the 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl (mcm5) and/or the 2-thio (s2) groups from the normal mcm5s2U34-state tRNA activates the GCN4-mediated pathway (Zinshteyn and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In yeast, loss of the threonyl-carbamoyl group from the normal t6A37-state tRNA activates the GCN4 response.
source: In yeast, loss of the threonyl-carbamoyl group from the normal t6A37-state tRNA also activates the GCN4 response (Thiaville et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In Drosophila, deficiency of the t6A37-state in a specific tRNA activates the target of rapamycin response.
source: In Drosophila, deficiency of the t6A37-state in a specific tRNA activates the target of rapamycin response (Rojas-Benitez et al., 2015), which reprograms gene expression in response to amino acid deficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In Neurospora, loss of the inosine (I) group from the normal I34-state tRNA activates the CPC-1 (cross-pathway-control-1) response.
source: In Neurospora, loss of the inosine (I) group from the normal I34-state tRNA activates the CPC-1 (cross-pathway-control-1) response, which is the ortholog of the yeast GCN4 response (Lyu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of the s2 group from the mcm5s2U34-state has been shown to reduce binding and accommodation of tRNA to the ribosomal A site and translocation to the P site.
source: Mechanistically, loss of the s2 group from the mcm5s2U34-state has been shown to reduce binding and accommodation of tRNA to the ribosomal A site and translocation to the P site (Ranjan and Rodnina, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of the s2 group from the related cmnm5s2U34-state in E. coli tRNAGln reduced tRNA aminoacylation and the subsequent binding and accommodation to the A site.
source: While we had previously shown that loss of the s2 group from the related cmnm5s2U34 (5-carboxy-amino-methyl-2-thio-uridine 34)-state in E. coli tRNAGln also reduced tRNA aminoacylation and the subsequent binding and accommodation to the A site (Rodriguez-Hernandez et al., 2013), we did not investigate the cellular response due to the deficiency in bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Over-expression of proS most effectively rescues cell viability in m1G37 deficiency.
source: The observation that over-expression of proS most effectively rescues cell viability in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 4D) indicates that aminoacylation of tRNAPro is a major determinant of cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Aminoacylation of tRNAPro is a major determinant of cell viability in m1G37 deficiency.
source: The observation that over-expression of proS most effectively rescues cell viability in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 4D) indicates that aminoacylation of tRNAPro is a major determinant of cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from rescue experiments.

claim: Loss of aminoacylation of tRNAPro is uniformly manifested at the Km (tRNA) step in m1G37 deficiency.
source: Notably, loss of aminoacylation of tRNAPro is uniformly manifested at the Km (tRNA) step in m1G37 deficiency (Figure 3—source data 1A), suggesting that the immediate proximity of the methylation to the aminoacylation-determinant anticodon G36 nucleotide is important for the bacterial ProRS.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by kinetic data in Figure 3—source data 1A.

claim: Human ProRS has diverged in tRNA recognition by shifting the emphasis toward the G35 nucleotide, which is more distant from m1G37.
source: In contrast, human ProRS has diverged in tRNA recognition by shifting the emphasis toward the G35 nucleotide, which is more distant from m1G37 (Burke et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The human ProRS enzyme may better accommodate m1G37-deficient tRNAs for aminoacylation.
source: This shift suggests the possibility that the human enzyme may better accommodate m1G37-deficient tRNAs for aminoacylation, and that the eukaryotic response to m1G37 deficiency is executed in a step other than aminoacylation for decoding at the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation based on the difference in tRNA recognition between bacterial and human ProRS.

claim: The eukaryotic response to m1G37 deficiency may be executed in a step other than aminoacylation for decoding at the A site.
source: This shift suggests the possibility that the human enzyme may better accommodate m1G37-deficient tRNAs for aminoacylation, and that the eukaryotic response to m1G37 deficiency is executed in a step other than aminoacylation for decoding at the A site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation.

claim: m1G37 is required for the ribosomal activity at the A site.
source: In summary, we show here that m1G37 is required for the ribosomal activity at the A site and that, when combined with previous studies, we emphasize the importance of m1G37 for the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Targeting TrmD can be explored in combination with antibiotics that target the A site (e.g., tetracycline, negamycin), those that target the translocation reaction (e.g., viomycin, spectinomycin), and those that target the P site (e.g., streptogramin A, bactobolin A, and retapamulin).
source: For example, targeting TrmD can be explored in combination of antibiotics that target the A site (e.g., tetracycline [Tet], negamycin), those that target the translocation reaction (e.g., viomycin, spectinomycin), and those that target the P site (e.g., streptogramin A, bactobolin A, and retapamulin) (Vázquez-Laslop and Mankin, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation about therapeutic strategies and supported by a citation.

claim: A combinatorial approach of targeting TrmD with other antibiotics may produce a synergistic and accelerated bactericidal effect that can combat the rapid emergence of multi-drug resistance of pathogens.
source: This combinatorial approach may produce a synergistic and accelerated bactericidal effect that can combat the rapid emergence of multi-drug resistance of pathogens.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation about therapeutic outcomes.

claim: The genes responsible for m1G37 biosynthesis are trmD in bacteria and trm5 in archaea and eukaryotes.
source: Interestingly, while m1G37 is conserved in evolution, the genes responsible for its biosynthesis are distinct – being trmD in bacteria and trm5 in archaea and eukaryotes (Christian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The protein products of trmD and trm5 are fundamentally different from each other in structure and mechanism.
source: The protein products of trmD and trm5 are fundamentally different from each other in structure and mechanism (Christian and Hou, 2007; Christian et al., 2010a; Christian et al., 2010b; Christian et al., 2016; Lahoud et al., 2011; Sakaguchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Expression of human trm5 is sufficient to supply m1G37-tRNAs to support bacterial viability in trmD-KO strains.
source: Upon induction with Ara, expression of human trm5 is sufficient to supply m1G37-tRNAs to support bacterial viability (trmD-KO (trm5+)) (Christian et al., 2004), whereas upon replacement of Ara with glucose (Glc), expression of human trm5 is arrested and the human enzyme is degraded inside bacterial cells (trmD-KO (trm5–)) (Christian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Upon replacement of Ara with glucose, expression of human trm5 is arrested and the human enzyme is degraded inside bacterial cells.
source: Upon induction with Ara, expression of human trm5 is sufficient to supply m1G37-tRNAs to support bacterial viability (trmD-KO (trm5+)) (Christian et al., 2004), whereas upon replacement of Ara with glucose (Glc), expression of human trm5 is arrested and the human enzyme is degraded inside bacterial cells (trmD-KO (trm5–)) (Christian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The level of methylation in the m1G37-state was high, reaching nearly 100% for E. coli tRNAPro(UGG) and nearly 70% for E. coli tRNAArg(CCG).
source: We confirmed that the level of methylation in the m1G37-state was high, reaching nearly 100% for the m1G37-state of E. coli tRNAPro(UGG) and nearly 70% for the m1G37-state of E. coli tRNAArg(CCG) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: m1G37 may be important for binding of each tRNAPro to ProRS.
source: The reduction in kcat/Km was driven by an increase in Km for all three tRNAs, indicating that m1G37 may be important for binding of each tRNA to ProRS (Figure 3—source data 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing increased Km values.

claim: m1G37 is immediately downstream of the two conserved anticodon nucleotides G35-G36, which are the major determinants of tRNAPro binding to ProRS.
source: This apparent binding defect makes sense structurally because m1G37 is immediately downstream of the two conserved anticodon nucleotides G35-G36, which are the major determinants of tRNAPro binding to ProRS (Cusack et al., 1998; Yaremchuk et al., 2000; Yaremchuk et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: All other post-transcriptional modifications played little or no role in aminoacylation of tRNAPro(UGG).
source: The critical role that m1G37 plays in the UGG isoacceptor was further highlighted by the finding that aminoacylation reaction with the m1G37-state tRNA has the same kcat/Km values as the native-state tRNA (Figure 3—source data 1A), indicating that all other post-transcriptional modifications played little or no role in aminoacylation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing kinetic parameters of m1G37-state and native-state tRNA.

claim: m1G37 contributed to catalysis of tRNAArg(CCG) aminoacylation.
source: This decrease was largely driven by a loss in kcat (Figure 3—source data 1A), indicating that m1G37 contributed to catalysis, which is a different effect than that observed for tRNAPro, where loss of m1G37 likely reduced tRNA binding to ProRS.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing decreased kcat.

claim: Other post-transcriptional modifications played a role in aminoacylation of tRNAArg(CCG).
source: Additionally, we observed a loss of 14.3-fold in kcat/Km from the native-state to the G37-state (Figure 3—source data 1A), greater than the 5.6-fold loss due to m1G37 alone, indicating that other post-transcriptional modifications played a role in aminoacylation of this tRNAArg, which also contrasts the observation that m1G37 alone is sufficient for rapid aminoacylation of tRNAPro.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the loss in kcat/Km between native-state to G37-state vs m1G37-state to G37-state.

claim: Loss of m1G37 reduces aminoacylation of all three isoacceptors of tRNAPro and the tRNAArg(CCG) isoacceptor, although by apparently different mechanisms.
source: Together, these results show that m1G37 is required for efficient aminoacylation of all three isoacceptors of tRNAPro and the tRNAArg(CCG) isoacceptor, and that loss of m1G37 reduces aminoacylation in all cases, although by apparently different mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the kinetic data presented.

claim: In contrast to aminoacylation, where all isoacceptors of tRNAPro were affected by loss of m1G37, loss of m1G37 only affected the overall reaction of dipeptide formation for one isoacceptor at one codon.
source: Thus, in contrast to aminoacylation, where all isoacceptors of tRNAPro were affected by loss of m1G37, loss of m1G37 only affected the overall reaction of dipeptide formation for one isoacceptor at one codon.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the effects on aminoacylation vs peptide-bond formation.

claim: For the single isoacceptor of tRNAArg, loss of m1G37 reduced the activity of both aminoacylation and the overall reaction of dipeptide formation at the A site.
source: Thus, for the single isoacceptor of tRNAArg, loss of m1G37 reduced the activity of both aminoacylation and the overall reaction of dipeptide formation at the A site.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the kinetic data for tRNAArg(CCG).

claim: The loss of aminoacylation of tRNAPro(UGG) and tRNAArg(CCG) is specific to m1G37 deficiency.
source: We confirmed that the loss of aminoacylation of these two tRNAs was specific to m1G37 deficiency.
evidence: This is confirmed by showing that a control tRNA not methylated by TrmD did not show loss of aminoacylation.

claim: The poor aminoacylation kinetics of m1G37-deficient tRNA can be overcome by increasing the corresponding aaRS enzyme.
source: This recovery indicates that the poor aminoacylation kinetics of m1G37-deficient tRNA can be overcome by increasing the corresponding aaRS enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that over-expression of proS and argS restored aminoacylation levels.

claim: m1G37 deficiency reduces the aminoacylation level of all tRNAPro species and tRNAArg(CCG) in vitro and in vivo.
source: Taken together, these findings show that m1G37 deficiency reduces the aminoacylation level of all tRNAPro species and tRNAArg(CCG) in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on in vitro kinetic assays and in vivo acid-urea gel analysis.

claim: Loss of aminoacylation levels in m1G37 deficiency compromises cell viability but can be overcome by over-expression of proS and to a lesser extent over-expression of argS.
source: This loss of aminoacylation levels compromises cell viability but can be overcome by over-expression of proS and to a lesser extent over-expression of argS.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the viability assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The magnitude of transcriptional changes was greater than that of translational changes in m1G37 deficiency.
source: Because the magnitude of transcriptional changes was greater than that of translational changes, yielding clearer results on which pathways are affected, we focused on the transcriptional changes arising from m1G37 deficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the results section comparing RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data.

claim: Translation of leuL serves as a sensitive genetic switch that has evolved to sense levels of aa-tRNAs and to respond to amino acid starvation by up-regulating the downstream biosynthetic pathways.
source: As with leader sequences of other amino acid biosynthesis operons (Kolter and Yanofsky, 1982), translation of leuL serves as a sensitive genetic switch that has evolved to sense levels of aa-tRNAs and to respond to amino acid starvation by up-regulating the downstream biosynthetic pathways (Wohlgemuth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Ribosome pausing at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in leuL during m1G37 deficiency reduced transcriptional termination of the downstream leuA gene.
source: These results support the notion that ribosome pausing at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in leuL during m1G37 deficiency reduced transcriptional termination of the downstream leuA gene (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced termination in Figure 5D.

claim: Strong pauses at two consecutive Pro codons CCA-CCG in ilvL could trigger anti-termination, explaining the higher RNA-seq levels of the downstream gene ilvG.
source: These strong pauses within the ilvL leader sequence could trigger anti-termination, explaining the higher RNA-seq levels of the downstream gene ilvG.
evidence: This is inferred from the ribosome profiling and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ilvG gene in strains derived from E. coli K12 MG1655 has a mutation that induces a frameshift midway through the gene, suggesting that it may be a pseudogene.
source: Notably, the ilvG gene in strains derived from E. coli K12 MG1655, such as the one used here, has a mutation that induces a frameshift midway through the gene, suggesting that it may be a pseudogene, although the ilvG gene appears intact in other E. coli strains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation about the specific strain used.

claim: Ribosome stalling at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in leuL prevents transcriptional termination and allows transcription of the downstream leuA-nLuc fusion.
source: Upon expression of the WT reporter construct, m1G37 deficiency in trmD-KO (trm5–) cells elevated the nLuc readout by 11.5-fold relative to control cells, consistent with the notion that ribosome stalling at the four consecutive Leu CUA codons in leuL prevents transcriptional termination and allows transcription of the downstream leuA-nLuc fusion.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Ribosome stalling at the Pro codons in ilvL activates expression of the downstream ilvG in m1G37 deficiency.
source: These results support the notion that ribosome stalling at the Pro codons in ilvL activates expression of the downstream ilvG in m1G37 deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Elevated proS expression restores aminoacylation levels of tRNAPro in cells, even in m1G37 deficiency, relieving ribosome stalling and repressing the downstream ilvG gene.
source: This result is consistent with the notion that elevated proS expression restores aminoacylation levels of tRNAPro in cells, even in m1G37 deficiency, relieving ribosome stalling and repressing the downstream ilvG gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing reduced ilvG activation upon proS over-expression in Figure 5G.

claim: The up-regulation of amino acid biosynthesis pathways suggests that they are activated by a genome-wide response due to ribosome stalling at Pro CCN, Arg CGG, and Leu CUA codons.
source: The up-regulation of these pathways suggests that they are activated by a genome-wide response due to ribosome stalling at Pro CCN, Arg CGG, and Leu CUA codons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression changes and ribosome profiling data.

claim: The increase in expression of the Cys biosynthesis pathway is correlated with the enrichment in gene ontology terms for genes involved in sulfate assimilation and hydrogen sulfide biosynthesis.
source: The increase in expression of the Cys biosynthesis pathway is correlated with the enrichment in gene ontology (GO) terms for genes involved in sulfate assimilation and hydrogen sulfide biosynthesis (Figure 5C) and is consistent with the notion that cysteine is synthesized from serine in bacteria by incorporation of sulfide to O-acetylserine (Kredich and Tomkins, 1966).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by GO analysis and a citation.

claim: Genes that are strongly induced or repressed by the stringent response are affected in a similar way by m1G37 deficiency.
source: Together, these results show that genes that are strongly induced or repressed by the stringent response are affected in a similar way by m1G37 deficiency, arguing that m1G37 deficiency induces changes in gene expression similar to those of the stringent response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on comparison of RNA-seq data with published stringent response data.

claim: The parallel changes in steady-state RNA levels between m1G37 deficiency and relA over-expression were remarkable, suggesting that loss of m1G37 triggers a response similar to that of the relA-dependent stringent response.
source: Collectively, the parallel changes in steady-state RNA levels between m1G37 deficiency and relA over-expression were remarkable, suggesting that loss of m1G37 triggers a response similar to that of the relA-dependent stringent response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comparison of gene expression changes.

claim: Because the glyoxylate cycle bypasses the decarboxylation reactions and instead replenishes TCA cycle intermediates, it is reasonable that these changes may be to build up metabolic intermediates for amino acid biosynthesis.
source: Notably, because the glyoxylate cycle bypasses the decarboxylation reactions and instead replenishes TCA cycle intermediates, it is reasonable that these changes may be to build up metabolic intermediates for amino acid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference about metabolic changes.

claim: This work demonstrates a previously unrecognized function of m1G37 that emphasizes its role throughout the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis.
source: This work demonstrates a previously unrecognized function of m1G37 that emphasizes its role throughout the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis, providing new insight into its essentiality for bacterial growth and survival.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the work's significance.

claim: This work provides new insight into the essentiality of m1G37 for bacterial growth and survival.
source: This work demonstrates a previously unrecognized function of m1G37 that emphasizes its role throughout the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis, providing new insight into its essentiality for bacterial growth and survival.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the work's significance.

claim: The importance of m1G37 for the ribosomal activity at the A site, together with its already demonstrated importance in maintaining the translational reading-frame from the A site to the P site and within the P site, establishes the involvement of the methylation throughout the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis.
source: The importance of m1G37 for the ribosomal activity at the A site, together with its already demonstrated importance in maintaining the translational reading-frame from the A site to the P site and within the P site (Gamper et al., 2021; Gamper et al., 2015a), establishes the involvement of the methylation throughout the entire elongation cycle of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: This sustained involvement of m1G37 during protein synthesis underscores its indispensable role in bacterial viability and survival.
source: This sustained involvement of m1G37 during protein synthesis underscores its indispensable role in bacterial viability and survival.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion about the significance of m1G37.
